newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions' new charter wins faint praise.
newsitem.headline: German unions' new charter wins faint praise.

text.p: Germany's trade unions won faint praise from the coalition government at the weekend after dropping Marxist rhetoric and moving closer towards the centre.

Delegates voted at an extraordinary meeting in Dresden of the Deutscher Gewerkschaftsbund (DGB), the umbrella body of German unions, to take an historic step forward, adopting a new charter which admits that market economics have led to "a high degree of material well-being".
The new charter promises to maintain and expand the welfare state, but the national executive failed in its demand for an unreserved declaration supporting a social market economy.
The new charter includes acceptance of the labour movement's sworn enemy -- market-based economics -- for the first time.

General Secretary of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), Peter Hintze, said he hoped the DGB would be constructive and offer pragmatic solutions to changes in the wage structure.

But he added that the CDU had committed itself to the development of a social market economy. "We call on the unions to work with it. If the DGB wants to speak for all workers, it must leave the language of class struggle behind".
The general secretary of the Free Democrats, the junior coaltion partners, took a harder line, attacking the unions for not going further.
In an interview with Welt am Sonntag newspaper, Guido Westerwelle said the market economy had "brought Germans more prosperity and more material security than ever before".
"The inability of the DGB to declare itself for the market economy is a part of its incapacity to follow a modern wages policy in the interests of the unemployed."
Debate on the charter lasted three days and at one point Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the metal and engineering union IG Metall, was accused of using threats to force it through.
The attacks demonstrated the lack of agreement among congress delegates on the draft of the new programme.

Some smaller unions wanted it to be postponed but Zwickel told delegates the passing of the new programme was the "concrete duty" for the congress and that, following the collapse of a job creation pact between unions and the government earlier this year, the time was ripe to do so.
DGB chairman Dieter Schulte told the conference: "The unions are determined to fight for work and social justice."
Delegates voted to include in the charter an obligation on unions to defend the social state and a re-affirmation of their right to use strikes.

The charter replaces an existing policy document, drawn up before the fall of eastern Europe's Communist governments, that is based heavily on the Marxist view that the interests of labour and capital are diametrically opposed.

But the ideological shift from Marx to market forces comes just as the unions, renowned for a restraint viewed as crucial to Germany's post-war economic success, gear up for one of their biggest showdowns yet with employers and government.
